guide.title: Red Hook, Brooklyn: Basins, Barges, and No Subway
guide.intro: The Lenape called this ground Ihpetonga, meaning a high point of sandy soil. Dutch colonists bought the land in 1636 and named it Roode Hoek for the reddish colour of the soil and the shape of the peninsula, and Red Hook became part of the town of Brooklyn in 1657 by order of Governor Peter Stuyvesant. The nineteenth century turned the peninsula into a working port. Daniel Richards, James S. T. Stranahan and William Beard built the Atlantic Basin, completed in 1850, and the Erie Basin, completed in 1864. Depression-era public works followed in quick succession: the Red Hook Play Center in 1936, the Red Hook Houses in 1939 and the Red Hook Recreational Area in 1940. The neighborhood still has no subway station of its own.

sections.heading: The basins, the barges, and the men who worked them
sections.body:
In 1848 the New York State Legislature funded converting Gowanus Creek into a commercial canal, linking Midwestern grain barges arriving by the Erie Canal to Red Hook's Erie Basin. At its industrial height the 1.5-mile canal saw as many as 26,000 barge passages in a single year.

Erie Basin itself was built from 1851 by William Beard with Jeremiah P. and George Robinson, who had begun buying waterfront land piecemeal from 1843. By the 1920s it was known as The Busiest Place in the Port of New York. It was sold to the Port of New York Authority in the 1950s as trucking and rail reduced demand, and today functions largely as an NYPD vehicle pound.

The dockworkers came in waves: Irish, German and Norwegian first, then Italian and Puerto Rican; African-American longshoremen began working the docks as early as the 1890s, and the Columbia Street area was a recognised Little Italy by the 1920s. In the 1880s a shantytown of roughly 2,000 squatters known as Slab City occupied the land between Hamilton Avenue and the waterfront.

The Depression brought a wave of public investment. The Red Hook Play Center opened in 1936 as the eleventh and last WPA pool to open in New York City; the Red Hook Houses, twenty buildings designed to accommodate 4,462 people, followed in 1939; the Red Hook Recreational Area opened in 1940.

sections.heading: The waterfront now
sections.body:
The late twentieth century was hard on Red Hook. In the 1990s Life magazine named it one of the worst neighborhoods in the United States and called it the crack capital of America. In 1992 Patrick Daly, the principal of P.S. 15, was killed in the crossfire of a drug-related shooting while searching for a student who had left school; the school was later renamed for him.

On June 18, 2008 a 346,000-square-foot IKEA opened at 1 Beard Street. Building it required filling and paving over the historic Red Hook graving dock, a nineteenth-century dry dock, and demolishing Civil War-era waterfront buildings. A city Economic Development Corporation report found that replacing the graving dock would cost roughly a billion dollars, and no replacement has been built.

Hurricane Sandy flooded the waterfront in October 2012. Sunny's Bar took extensive flooding and structural damage and stayed shut until September 2013.

The next chapter is already drafted. In September 2025 a community task force voted to approve a $3.5 billion Brooklyn Marine Terminal Vision Plan for the Red Hook waterfront, calling for up to 6,000 apartments, 40 percent of them permanently affordable.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Red Hook has no subway station.

NYC Ferry's South Brooklyn route calls at the Red Hook/Atlantic Basin landing, at Ferris Street and Clinton Wharf.

Two bus routes reach the neighborhood. The B61 travels through Red Hook via 9th Street, Van Brunt Street and Columbia Street, continuing along Atlantic Avenue into Downtown Brooklyn at one end and to a Windsor Terrace terminus at 20th Street and Prospect Park West at the other. The B57 terminates in Red Hook at Beard Street and Otsego Street, and runs the other way to 61st Street and Flushing Avenue in Maspeth, Queens.

The nearest subway stations are in other neighborhoods and should be treated as such. Smith-9th Streets, on the F and G, is over the Gowanus Canal near the intersection of Smith and Ninth Streets, in Gowanus. Carroll Street, also on the F and G, is in Carroll Gardens at Carroll and Smith Streets.

faq.question: How do I get to Red Hook without a subway?
faq.answer: By ferry or by bus. NYC Ferry's South Brooklyn route calls at the Red Hook/Atlantic Basin landing at Ferris Street and Clinton Wharf. The B61 runs through the neighborhood via Van Brunt and Columbia Streets, and the B57 terminates at Beard Street and Otsego Street. The nearest subway stations, Smith-9th Streets and Carroll Street, are in Gowanus and Carroll Gardens respectively.

faq.question: Where does the name Red Hook come from?
faq.answer: From the Dutch Roode Hoek, the name colonists gave the land they bought in 1636, for the reddish colour of the soil and the shape of the peninsula jutting into New York Harbor. The Lenape name for the same ground was Ihpetonga, a high point of sandy soil.

faq.question: Is there a hotel in Red Hook?
faq.answer: No hotel is listed here, and lodging should be treated as effectively unavailable inside Red Hook. No hotel from a neighboring neighborhood is named in its place.

faq.question: What happened to the Red Hook graving dock?
faq.answer: It was filled and paved over to build the IKEA store that opened at 1 Beard Street on June 18, 2008, along with the demolition of Civil War-era waterfront buildings. A city Economic Development Corporation report put the cost of replacing the dock at roughly a billion dollars, and no replacement has been built.

faq.question: Can visitors go aboard the Waterfront Museum barge?
faq.answer: Yes. The Waterfront Museum is housed aboard the Lehigh Valley Railroad Barge No. 79 at 290 Conover Street and offers free tours on most Thursdays from 4 to 8pm and Saturdays from 1 to 5pm.

photos.title: Timber piers and a brick warehouse
photos.description: Derelict timber piers ring a basin at sunset, with a brick warehouse on the left and a harbour crane on the right.
photos.author: Original photography by Nightscream; stitched by Marku1988

photos.title: The Red Hook war memorial doughboy
photos.description: A bronze soldier raises his helmet in front of a brick wall hung with flags and covered in named memorial plaques.
photos.author: Rhododendrites

photos.title: Sunny's Bar on Conover Street
photos.description: A striped awning lettered SUNNY'S BAR over a dark storefront, with wooden benches and a neon sign, on a wet cobbled street.
photos.author: Tessa Bury

places.name: Coffey Park
places.address: Verona Street between Richard Street and Dwight Street, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A neighborhood park with playgrounds, basketball and handball courts, barbecuing areas and a dog-friendly area.
places.history: Named for Michael J. Coffey, the Cork-born alderman and state senator who was instrumental in creating Red Hook's park and who served in the U.S. Navy aboard the gunboat Monticello during the Civil War. Coffey Street carries his name too.

places.name: Red Hook Recreation Area
places.address: Halleck Street and Bush Street between Otsego Street and Court Street, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A large recreation complex with an Olympic-size outdoor pool, a running track, soccer and baseball fields, a playground and a recreation centre with cardio equipment and exercise classes.
places.history: Opened in 1940, the last of the three Depression-era projects that also produced the Red Hook Play Center in 1936 and the Red Hook Houses in 1939. The landmarked Play Center pool complex stands within it.

places.name: Louis J. Valentino, Jr. Park and Pier
places.address: Ferris Street between Coffey Street and Van Dyke Street, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A waterfront pier park on the site of former shipping piers, with open views across Buttermilk Channel toward Governors Island and Lower Manhattan. It is used for public events.
places.history: Named for an FDNY firefighter, Louis J. Valentino, Jr.

places.name: Red Hook Play Center (Sol Goldman Pool)
places.summary: Still an operating public pool inside the Red Hook Recreation Area, and an individual New York City Landmark covering the bath house, pool, former diving pool, bleachers, comfort station, storage house and perimeter fencing.
places.history: Constructed 1934-36 by Joseph L. Hautman and others, with Aymar Embury II as consulting architect, on a landfill site between the former Erie Basin and the Gowanus Bay. It opened in 1936 as the eleventh and last WPA pool to open in New York City, and was designated a landmark on November 18, 2008 as LP-2241.

places.name: Waterfront Museum
places.summary: A maritime and railroad history museum housed aboard a wooden railroad barge, open on most Thursdays from 4 to 8pm and Saturdays from 1 to 5pm for free tours.
places.history: The vessel is the Lehigh Valley Railroad Barge No. 79, built in 1914 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places at Red Hook on June 2, 2015, after an earlier 1989 listing at a berth in New Jersey.

places.name: Pioneer Works
places.summary: A nonprofit cultural centre for art, music, science and technology, with galleries and a garden open Wednesday to Sunday, 12 to 6pm.
places.history: The building was built in 1866 for Pioneer Iron Works.

places.name: Brooklyn Cruise Terminal
places.summary: A 180,000-square-foot cruise terminal on Buttermilk Channel, converted from a 1954 freight terminal. Ships from Carnival Corporation, which owns Cunard and Princess Cruises, call it their home port.
places.history: It opened on April 15, 2006, with the inaugural arrival of the Queen Mary 2.

places.name: Widow Jane Distillery
places.summary: A working whiskey and rum distillery offering public tours on Fridays at 4pm and Saturdays and Sundays at 1pm, 3pm and 5pm, at $27 per person. Its tasting-room bar, Botanica, is open Fridays from 5 to 10pm and weekends from 2 to 10pm.

places.name: Sunny's Bar
places.summary: A waterfront bar still open under Tone Balzano Johansen, known for its Sundays at Sunny's live-music and reading gatherings.
places.history: Founded in 1890 as John's Bar and Restaurant, serving sailors and stevedores, and made a neighborhood cultural hub under Antonio 'Sunny' Balzano in the 1990s. It took extensive flooding and structural damage in the October 2012 storm and reopened in September 2013.

photos.title: Sunny's Bar on Conover Street
photos.description: A striped awning lettered SUNNY'S BAR over a dark storefront, with wooden benches and a neon sign, on a wet cobbled street.
photos.author: Tessa Bury

places.name: Defonte's Sandwich Shop
places.summary: An Italian hero counter still run by the founding family, with Nick's grandson Nicky at the helm.
places.history: Founded in 1922 by Nick Defonte for Red Hook longshoremen. It featured in the Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives episode 'Long Standing Legacies' on February 20, 2012.

places.name: Hometown Bar-B-Que
places.summary: A Texas-style barbecue restaurant on Van Brunt Street, open every day except Monday, from noon.

places.name: Red Hook Lobster Pound
places.summary: A lobster roll restaurant open seven days a week for indoor dining, takeout and delivery. Its outdoor Lobster Shack seating closes for the winter.

entries.name: Louis J. Valentino, Jr. Park and Pier
entries.note: Built on the site of former shipping piers, with open water views across Buttermilk Channel to Governors Island and Lower Manhattan.

entries.name: Coffey Park
entries.note: Red Hook's neighborhood green, named for the Cork-born alderman who was instrumental in creating it.

entries.name: Red Hook Recreation Area
entries.note: Ballfields, a track and an Olympic-size pool, opened in 1940 as the last of the neighborhood's three Depression-era projects.

entries.name: Red Hook Play Center
entries.note: The eleventh and last WPA pool to open in New York City, landmarked in 2008 and still swimming.

entries.name: Waterfront Museum
entries.note: A museum aboard a 1914 wooden railroad barge, free to visit on most Thursday evenings and Saturday afternoons.

entries.name: Pioneer Works
entries.note: Art, music, science and technology under one roof, in a building put up in 1866 for Pioneer Iron Works.

entries.name: Brooklyn Cruise Terminal
entries.note: Converted from a 1954 freight terminal and opened in 2006 with the arrival of the Queen Mary 2.

entries.name: Widow Jane Distillery
entries.note: A working whiskey and rum distillery on Conover Street with scheduled public tours and the Botanica tasting room.

entries.name: Sunny's Bar
entries.note: Serving this waterfront since 1890, flooded by Sandy and back open since September 2013.

entries.name: Defonte's Sandwich Shop
entries.note: Italian heroes made for longshoremen since 1922, still run by the Defonte family.

entries.name: Hometown Bar-B-Que
entries.note: Texas-style barbecue on Van Brunt Street, closed Mondays.

entries.name: Red Hook Lobster Pound
entries.note: Lobster rolls year-round on Van Brunt Street, with the outdoor Lobster Shack seating shut over winter.
